utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. The Prosecution has a new member of the trial team in this case who is appearing today for the first time, Mr. Stefan Waespi. Also appearing for the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic lead counsel, Stefan Bourgon co-counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber bids good morning to all those present, and in particular the new arrival, Mr. Stefan Waespi, on the Prosecution side. I also bid good morning to the Defence attorneys, the accused, and all the personnel of this courtroom. Today we have one witness planned, who should appear in the next few minutes, but the Prosecution wishes to make a comment, and we'll go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, will you please bring in our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me check that you're hearing me in your own language. If so, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called as a witness for the Defence, and before you make your solemn declaration, will you please tell us your first and last name, your date and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Hazim Barucija, born on the 2nd of January, 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Lasva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a job today? If so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm working in the elementary school in Janjici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. In the primary school. And in 1992, 1993, were you employed; and, if so, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was employed in the same school. At the time I was director of the school, or principal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were director in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you testified before in an international or national court about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993 or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified before. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'm going to give you some information so as to make sure that the proceedings proceed smoothly and that you can testify in a relaxed manner. Being a school principal, you certainly have some idea of what a trial is like. The trial and the proceedings before this Tribunal take place in the following manner: You will first have to answer questions that will be put to you by the representatives of the accused, whom you have certainly met, and they are seated to your left. This would normally last between one and one and a half hours. At the end of that period of questions, what is known as the examination-in-chief, the Prosecution, which is seated to your right, will also have questions which will take the same amount of time, one hour to one and a half hours, and this is called the cross-examination. And you will notice that the form the questions will take will not be quite the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. same as those put by the Defence. At the end of this stage, the attorneys for the Defence may have additional questions for you linked to those during the cross-examination. The three Judges in front of you may also have questions for you, and they may put them to you at any point of time. But to make sure that the proceedings run smoothly, we prefer to wait until the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination, and re-examination is over to ask our questions. We will normally be putting our questions towards the end of your testimony. If the questions appear to you to be too complicated, please ask the person putting them to rephrase them, because the questions will relate to a period that was more than ten years ago, so you may have forgotten certain things. Answer if you're quite sure of yourself. If you're less sure, tell the person putting the question whether you remember well or not so well, because it is very important to know that as far as you're concerned, we have nothing in writing from you, so it is only your oral answers that will be used by us; hence the importance of your answers. I also need to inform you of two other points, which I do for all witnesses, regardless of who they may be. You have just made the solemn declaration to tell the whole truth, which excludes all false testimony. As a teacher, you must know that false testimony is an offence, and that offence can be punished in this Tribunal. And another point which certainly doesn't apply to you, but I still wish to draw your attention to it: When a witness needs to answer a question, should he consider that that answer could possibly incriminate him in another proceeding, the witness may say, "I don't wish to answer that question." That exists in our Rules and also in the legislation of many countries. This is quite an exceptional situation. The Chamber may, nevertheless, instruct the witness to answer, but you will be granted immunity. In American law, immunity is granted by the Prosecution, but according to this procedure, it is the Chamber who grants you immunity. I'm just telling you of this, though it is something that we have not encountered so far. If in the course of the examination you have any difficulty of any kind, please let us know. Don't hesitate. I also wish to tell you that we will be having two breaks in the morning to allow you to take a rest, because the examination may be quite exhausting, but also for technical reasons, because of the tapes that need to be changed every hour and a half. As we begin at 9.00, the break will be at 10.30, and the break will be 25 to 30 minutes. So I've conveyed to you all the information that I wish to. The Defence will add something else, but I leave that to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Barucija.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you've just heard from the Presiding Judge, I'm going to ask you one more thing. You and I speak the same language. Therefore, you would be able to answer my question as soon as you hear it. However, my question and your answer have to be interpreted for the Trial Chamber and everybody else in the courtroom. This is very important, because you are here to testify before this Trial Chamber. That is why I'm -- would like to ask you to make a pause after my question, wait for the interpretation to be over, and answer after that. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've told us you were born in Lasva. Where did you reside before the war? Where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Up to 1994, I resided in Lasva. I lived there for 40 years, and then I moved to Zenica, where I currently reside.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've also told us that you work in an elementary school. What are you by profession, and where did you acquire your grades, your education?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I'm a teacher. I teach classes from first to fourth, and I graduated from the teachers academy in Travnik, in a town which is some 40 kilometres from the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, for how many years did you work in the primary school in Lasva?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I worked there from 1974, and I have never worked anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, where is Lasva? Which municipality does Lasva belong to?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Lasva is between Zenica, Kakanj, and Busovaca. It is the local -- the last local commune on the south of Zenica municipality, and it belongs to the municipality of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When we say Lasva, do we only imply a village or do we also imply a local commune?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I'm referring to the entire local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what other villages belong to that local commune?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Lasva with the hamlets called Sajtovici, and Rajici. Dusina village with hamlets called Kegelj and Brdo. Donja Visnjica, Gornja Visnjica, and Dolipolje village with its hamlet Bozici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, who resided in Lasva before the war? What was the ethnic composition of that local commune?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: There were Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats. According to the ethnic structure and according to the 1991 census, if I can remember well, there were between 70 and 75 per cent Bosniaks, and there were between 12 and 15 per cent Croats and Serbs respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship among the villagers, and what was your relationship with your Croat and Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: We lived well with our neighbours, Serbs and Croats. Our relationships were good. If anybody came from outside, they wouldn't be able to spot any difference in terms of our ethnic origin. I personally had a very good relationship with both of these ethnic groups in respect of my profession. I was even closer to some of my Croat neighbours and to my Bosniak neighbours. I had a lot of friends among Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that the local commune of Lasva has three neighbouring -- actually two neighbouring communities, Busovaca and Kakanj. Can you tell us which villages and hamlets border on the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Dusina village with Kegelj and Brdo hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the mixed population of the entire local commune, could you please tell me, what was the ethnic make-up of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: In Dusina, there were only Bosniaks. In Kegelji, there were Croats, and they were two or three Serb families there, and in Brdo there were a few Bosniak families and a few Croat families. The distance between those two hamlets is about a kilometre to a kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, the local commune of Lasva, is it significant in any respect when we're talking about the general region of Central Bosnia or the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Our local commune, up to 1972, was a railroad junction, a very important railroad junction. There was a railroad leading to Jajce passing through Lasva. So Lasva was a -- the main railroad hub. When the road was built two kilometres away from the entrance to Lasva, a big crossroad was built on that main road and this crossroad was very important in state terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness be shown two maps that I will be using during his testimony. These two maps that I am about to present to the witness are already in evidence. The scale of the first map is 10:25000, and the number is DH1 to 14, and the second one is DH90. This is a section depicting this region, and it has been taken from a map, the scale of which is 1:50000. And this map, the latter, is our Defence Exhibit 90. I may have been speaking very fast. There are wrong numbers in the transcript. The map one is DH104, and DH105. DH104 is the section 42, and DH105 depicts the section 44.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, can you please take the map on which it says Dusina set four, 1:50000, and I would kindly ask you to take a marker from the usher and try and draw the borders of your local commune, if these can be seen on this map.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now on the border draw a circle, marking it by number 1. This is how we will know that this circle represents the borders of Lasva local commune. It doesn't matter where you're going to draw this circle. You just draw the circle, draw two arrows on each side of the circle and put number 1.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: You want me to make a circle around the border?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, just a small circle that will serve to put number 1 into that circle, and on that border itself draw an arrow so as to show us that this number 1 refers to the border of the local commune of Lasva.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you please show me the part where the local commune of Lasva borders on Busovaca municipality. Draw another line to show where your local commune borders on the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I believe that it is up to here. And further on towards east, this is already Kakanj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would also kindly ask you to draw another circle, put a number 2 next to it, and for the transcript, it will be marked that this is the border of your local community with Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Barucija, on this same map, can you please mark the seat of the local commune of Lasva. Do it by drawing a circle and putting number 3 in it. This is going to denote the seat of your local commune.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I will also ask you, Mr. Barucija, to draw another circle and put number 4 in it to mark the strategic point of national interest, the so-called Lasva junction.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, number 1 denotes the borders of Lasva; number 2 denotes the place where Lasva borders on Busovaca; number 3 is the seat of the local commune of Lasva; and number 4 is the Lasva junction. Thank you very much. We will continue your testimony. Mr. Barucija, what links and with what towns existed for the villagers of your local commune?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: All of our inhabitants, regardless of their ethnic background, had the only link with Zenica. That was their only link.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What does that imply? Where did they go to school? Where did they work? Where did they do anything else that was important for the life of every citizen?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Once they finished primary school, those who wanted to go to secondary school had to go to Zenica. I'm one of the very few exceptions. I went to the secondary school in Travnik. So everybody went to Zenica to continue their education. Everybody worked in Zenica in production or non-production company. It would be a very rare case for somebody to work somewhere else and not in Zenica. There were a few cases of people who went to the secondary school in Sarajevo if such schools did not exist in Zenica. For example, the secondary traffic school did not exist in Zenica, but most of the population -- 99 per cent of the population went to school and worked in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, what were the roads to Zenica like? Was it easy to get to Zenica from your local commune?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it was. We had railroad, and it took some 15 minutes for us to get to Zenica. There was also a road. There were buses. There was a regular bus service, and it took only about 15 minutes to get to Zenica by car or by bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were the links of your local community with Busovaca municipality? How easy and simple was it to get to that municipality?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: One could get from Lasva to Busovaca only by road, only by using private vehicles. There was one bus a day from Lasva to Busovaca, only on Saturday, because Busovaca has an open market on Saturday. There was no railroad, and there were no other connections for the -- for our villagers with Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, did the Croatian population of that region have any connection with Busovaca at all?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As for education and work are concerned, there was nothing. The only links that they had with Busovaca was a religious link. I believe that they belonged to the parish office in Busovaca, and that's where they went to church.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, at the beginning of war, did the population of Lasva get militarily organised? Did people respond to the general mobilisation call, and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: After the general mobilisation call, it was mostly the Bosniaks that responded. They were the ones who wanted to join the Territorial Defence. However, there was an objective problem in terms of the fact that there was no arms available. Serbs did not wish to join such units. Croats were partly sitting on the fence, and they were saying that there was no need for them to join. They were not so very categorical in -- in refusing to join the territorial units as the Serbs were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice at any point in time that the Croatian population organised themselves militarily in a different way? If you did, can you tell us what happened? How were they organised?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: At the beginning of April, as soon as the war broke out and -- I believe that this was on the first or second day of Bajram, the Muslim holiday, I was not in Lasva. I was in Janjici, in the school there. I heard that on that day, Dario Kordic came to Lasva, that the Croats rallied around him. There was some 20 or 30 of them. They armed themselves with infantry weapons. It was their intention to establish a unit of the Croatian Defence Council. It was at the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, this HVO unit, which brigade did it become part of?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, it became part of the Busovaca HVO Brigade, because their commander had constant contacts with Busovaca. He was in Busovaca on a daily basis, and I believe that their command was there, which means that they belonged to the Busovaca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who their commander was?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: It was Zvonko Rajic. He was the commander of the HVO unit in Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, did there come a time when you joined some armed forces; and which forces were those?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: In April, May, up to the 20th of June in the territory of our local commune, there was no regular army formations of the Territorial Defence. There was just this HVO unit, which didn't bother most of the population, as far as I know. I personally was satisfied that at least those neighbours armed themselves and we could feel a certain degree of safety because they patrolled the area of the commune with those arms on a daily basis. This gave us a certain sense of safety, because none of the Bosniaks had arms. Serbs had arms, but they had not used it up to then. In June of that year, after the JNA unit left the barracks in Zenica, the arms were placed under the control of the Territorial Defence, and then the Territorial Defence gave our local commune some 20 or 25 pieces of infantry weapons. Those were mostly M-48 rifles, several semi-automatic rifles, some antiquated Russian automatic rifles. And it is only then that we formed a platoon consisting of some 20 to 25 members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you join that platoon? Did you have a position in that platoon? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't join this platoon, because before that, I had been appointed as the president of the Crisis Staff in Lasva. The president was Nezir Brkic, at the very beginning, in April up to mid-May. For some health reason he wanted to be relieved of that duty, and that is when I took over as the president of the Crisis Staff, and I remained in that position up to the end of August, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the month of August 1992, did you join the Territorial Defence, and did you have a position within the Territorial Defence after that?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: During the month of August, in the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Zenica, there were very intense activities aimed at establishing sector staffs. On the left bank of Bosnia, we formed a so-called Bosnia detachment, which became operational in September. I was then appointed a commander of that detachment, which became operational in September. It was after then that I became engaged in the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which local communes were covered by that detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: This detachment covered the local communes of Lasva, Janjici, Drivusa and Raspotocje, which means the entire left bank of the River Bosna from the border on the south, which was Lasva, up to Zenica itself. The entire area is about 15 kilometres on the left bank of the River Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, tell me, did there come a time in 1992 when there was some misunderstandings between this detachment of the Territorial Defence and the HVO unit, or in other words, did the relationship between the Croatian and Muslim populations deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: There were no special tensions between Bosniaks and Croats up to the moment when the Territorial Defence platoon was established in June. When the Territorial Defence platoon was established and when some of the Bosniaks took arms, and when we started controlling and securing the territory of the local commune, some sort of incidents which were not serious did take place. It was not serious, but the situation from then on was not as it had been before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, did the HVO accept the fact that Bosniaks also organised themselves within their legitimate military structures, or did they express some reservations against this?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They accepted the fact that the Territorial Defence platoon had been formed. At that time, I was the president of the Crisis Staff. This Crisis Staff was mixed. It consisted of the representatives of the Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks. The majority were Bosniaks because of the ethnic structure. We met on a daily basis in order to deal with everyday problems. We also called -- we asked the representatives of the HVO and asked them to have a joint unit, whatever it may have been called, but we wanted to have one unit with one commander and one deputy commander. One of them would be a Croat, the other one would be a Muslim. We wanted for us to act jointly; however, they did not accept our proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, did there come a time when you started experiencing communication problems? Were obstacles placed on the roads? And if this did happen, who was it who did it and in which places?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: When the Bosniak detachment was established in September -- in the September of 1992, the first thing we did was to secure the Lasva junction. We placed it under our control. We blocked exits from Zenica and Sarajevo or -- and we channeled everybody through one checkpoint. That's where we controlled traffic, and we secured the area. When we established that checkpoint in response, the HVO put up a checkpoint at the very entrance to Lasva, on the railroad. They asked us not to control traffic on the Lasva junction. In our view, this was inconceivable, and we could not accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which was you superior command at that time?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Our superior command at the time was the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, did there come a time when there were changes in the Municipal Staff? Were there also changes in the Territorial Defence in your area?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: These detachments were active in September, October, and November. When the 3rd Corps was established with a headquarters in Zenica, these detachments were also reorganised, and these detachments became three anti-sabotage detachments; the 1st, the 2nd, and the 3rd Anti-Sabotage Detachments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which one did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: We belonged to the 2nd Anti-Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a military position then?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: With the formation of the 2nd Anti-Sabotage Detachment, I became deputy commander of that detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Barucija, what is the main task of the so-called anti-sabotage detachments in those days, and of your detachment in particular?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: The name itself speaks for itself. It means that its main task was to prevent any sabotage activities or incursions within the zone of responsibility of the detachment, to secure facilities of strategic importance, and to have control over the territory. Combat activities were not a priority task of these detachments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who were the members of your detachment? Were they people with military training or what kind of manpower did you have in that detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: The detachment was formed of members of former detachments, Bosnian, Kubar, Kocevo, there were several such detachments, and as far as I know, none of the members were active duty military officers. They were all volunteers, people who certainly did not have sufficient military knowledge, but for patriotic reasons would accept any assignments they were given.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answering my questions a moment ago, you said that the HVO, in response to your establishing the checkpoint to secure the crossroads, that they also set up checkpoints. Tell us, in December, where did the HVO set up its checkpoints? Would you like to show it to us on the map? If so, use the other map that is to the scale 1:25000. Would you mark that position with P1, checkpoint 1.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand what you have written correctly, it means that the HVO set up five checkpoints within the territory of your local commune; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, in the course of the month of January. When we set up our checkpoint at the Lasva crossroads, they formed a checkpoint at the entrance to the local commune, at the railway station itself, which I have marked as P1. And that went on like that throughout. Then in January, as the situation became increasingly tense on the front in Busovaca and Vitez, they didn't set up checkpoints to obstruct traffic, but they did control the traffic. There were usually two men checking the traffic passing. P2 at the entrance to the hamlet of Rajici, inhabited exclusively by Croats; P3 at the crossroads between Gornja and Donja Visnjica; P4 at the -- where the road turned off for Brdo, where several Croat families lived; and P5 in the village of Dusina where the road leads off to the hamlet of Kegelji.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Barucija, in view of the duty that you had as commander of this Anti-Sabotage Detachment, did you know whether it was possible in January to move freely from Zenica to Busovaca, passing through the crossroads and then from then on to Travnik? Was it possible to move in that way?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: One could travel normally from Zenica to the Lasva crossroads. From that crossroads to Travnik you could go as far as Grablje and Gavrine Kuce, as far as I know, and from there on units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina could not pass along that route towards Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, which was then the only available route from Zenica to free territory under the control of the army in the vicinity of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: The only road link between the capital, that is Sarajevo, and the Zenica valley was the highway M17, going from Sarajevo to Zenica. And where the Lasva joins the Bosna River, we strengthened security at the crossroads and the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that route was captured by Serb forces in one segment, and you said also that one couldn't move along the Lasva River valley, what was the only possibility of reaching the environs of Sarajevo and free territory?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Going from the direction of Lasva and Zenica, one could reach Sarajevo only if you used the highway passing through the Lasva crossroads. From Busovaca municipality, from villages mostly inhabited by Bosniaks, Solakovici, Sudine, et cetera, you could travel through Dusina, you see. And then this whole route via Lasva to the Lasva crossroads and from there on to Zenica and Sarajevo. So that was the only chance of the Bosniaks from Busovaca to use this road to reach other free territories in Sarajevo, Zenica, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To what extent the formation of checkpoints that you have now marked led to problems with -- for the Territorial Defence and the population in Dusina and the other areas that you have just mentioned in terms of travel?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: These checkpoints actually prevented Bosniaks from Busovaca municipality to move around normally, because there was control or checks by members of the HVO at all the crossroads or roads leading to their settlements. I can give you an example from October 1992. A TAM with a mortar, I don't know what calibre, set off from Solakovici, and at the checkpoint P5, by radio communications, I don't know exactly which, P2 was informed that this small van had passed with a mortar and that they should capture it down there when it arrives. I was told that there were certain problems at the P2 checkpoint and that we should come and investigate. Members of the HVO told us that they had stopped a TAM van with a mortar there, asking where it was going. We had a discussion for some time. We felt that regardless of where it was going, it was going to the front against a common aggressor, because that was our position, and we saw no reason why they should stop it. They should let it go to the front. If you don't want to go to war, don't prevent us from doing it. At some point, I think it was Zvonko Rajic's father reported by radio in Busovaca that they had captured a van with a mortar. And after some half hour of discussion and debate, a jeep arrived from Busovaca, five to six men in black uniforms came out - that was the first time for me to see them - and they asked where the mortar is. And they said the mortar had already left, because we somehow managed to let the driver leave together with the mortar. He probably went to free territory somewhere in Busovaca. And Zvonko's father, Igo [phoen], cocked his gun at his brother Marko, saying why he behaved in that way and why he wouldn't allow soldiers of the army to move freely along that route? He pointed his gun at his own brother, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Barucija. Tell me, did a part of your Anti-Sabotage Detachment, at some point in time was it engaged elsewhere? And as a result, which forces were left behind within the territory of the local commune?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I think it was around the 10th of January that our detachment had to send a platoon to the Maglaj front to assist units in Maglaj that were securing the territory against the Chetniks because they were constantly shelling and endeavouring to capture Maglaj. So a number of members of the 2nd Anti-Sabotage Detachment were sent to the front in Maglaj, and these were mostly members coming from our own local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the fact that a part of your members left to another quite distant area, did this make it necessary to engage some other units to assist in securing the Lasva crossroads?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: When our members left for Maglaj, the Lasva crossroads was left unattended, virtually unattended. And the detachment commander informed the Municipal Staff which, probably in communication with the 3rd Corps, found a solution for this, and as a replacement for the soldiers who had left for Maglaj, the corps command, as far as I know, resubordinated to the Municipal Staff a company from the 7th Muslim Brigade, whose main task was to continue to protect and secure the Lasva crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, were you absent for a period, and why, from the territory of the local commune?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I was absent for a number of days. I think it was between the 17th and the 22nd of January. The Staff Command ordered me to go to the Maglaj front to tour the fighters there, because they were rather scared. So that I was meant to calm them down, to encourage them, because actually that was their first encounter with actual battle. Until then, our members had not participated in battle, in fighting, they had just secured facilities. And I stayed there, I think, for four to five days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned, Mr. Barucija, this company that had come to assist, was it already securing the Lasva crossroads?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: When I returned from Maglaj, yes, the company from the 7th Muslim Brigade was stationed at the Lasva crossroads together with a company command in the house of Anto Miladin, a Serb, who gave us this house to use -- to be used by the Bosnian detachment to protect the Lasva crossroads. So their command was housed there, and they took over full responsibility for securing the Lasva crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Shortly after your return, Mr. Barucija, were you confronted with combat activities in the immediate vicinity of your local commune? And, if so, tell us where those operations were taking place between the army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I believe that on the 24th of January, active combat activities started in the territory of Busovaca municipality. On that day, I came from the detachment command, which was in Zenica. I came to the headquarters of the company of the 7th Muslim Brigade to see whether there were any problems with our own members who were left with them, to assist them, to give them certain instructions, because these were people who were not from the area, who didn't know the area. So I stayed there for a short while. I think it must have been between 8.00 and 9.00 a.m. that intensive shelling started of the village of Merdani, which is within the territory of Busovaca municipality. And this shelling went on for about -- until about 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, will you now show on the 25000 -- no, I'm sorry, the 50000 scale map - the one you used a moment ago - would you mark with a circle the locality that was shelled.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And will you put the letter M inside so we can know that it is Merdani that is in question.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, how far is Merdani from Lasva?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As the crow flies, maybe two kilometres. But by road, I think it's about three kilometres to the crossroads, and to Lasva itself about another two kilometres. Therefore, a total of five if one would use the roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the beginning of the intensive shelling of Merdani, did some people arrive in Lasva, or how in fact did you know what was going on in Merdani?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As we were here at the confluence of the Lasva and Bosna Rivers where the company headquarters was by the -- the distance is not even two kilometres. We could hear the shelling of the village. It could be heard very well. Sometime in the afternoon, between 3.00 and 4.00, there was a column of people moving along this road from Travnik to Zenica. There's the village of Grablje using this road. There was a column of people, and we spoke to them about what was happening, and they said that their village was being shelled all day, that there was infantry fighting. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those people were heading towards Zenica. Some of them went to Lasva, others went to Janjici, depending on where people had acquaintances, friends, or relatives. What happened, actually, was an exodus of the population of Merdani.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of this situation and the closeness of the combat operations and the fact that the population was fleeing the village en masse, did you, as deputy commander of the Anti-Sabotage Detachment, feel it to be your duty to inform anyone, or did you do anything at all?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As we virtually had no means of communication, I asked the deputy company commander from our own detachment that we use his passenger car to go to the corps command to see whether they had any information about what was happening on the ground, and if not, for us to tell them about it and for the corps to take appropriate steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you reach the corps? Where did you go and what happened?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived at the corps. I think we found the duty operations officer. We asked him whether they had any information about what was happening on the ground in the immediate vicinity of the Lasva crossroads. He said that he had heard something, but he just waved his head, he said he didn't know anything with reliability. Then we informed him in detail that the village had been shelled, village of Merdani had been shelled virtually all day and that the population had left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Barucija, on the 25th of January, in the village of Dusina itself, were there any incidents? Had you heard about them? Had there been any arrests or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I was not within the territory of the local commune on that day, that is the 25th, but I heard later on that two members of the army had been captured, in a sense, when they were moving through the village. I don't know exactly where they were going nor what they were doing, but we received no report in the military sense because they were not members of our detachment. But I don't think there was any special problem, because the men were released during the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you or did you know that on that day, the 25th of January, there was an armed conflict in the village of Dusina and that all Croatian houses were set on fire on that day?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, on the 25th of January there were no conflicts whatsoever and, therefore, no torchings either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge that there had been a slaughter of Croatian women, children, and the elderly in the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: If there had been no conflicts, then it's absurd to talk about any slaughter, which is much worse. There were no conflicts on the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps this would be a suitable moment for the break, so that after that I can move on to questions relating to the 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is twenty-five past ten, and we will resume at about five to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, after your return from the command of the 3rd Corps on that night of the 25th to the area where the command of the detachment guarding the junction was, did any other units also come there? And if they did, did you know what their task was?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of our detachment, during that evening, that is after we received information from the 3rd Corps, a unit from the strength of the 303rd Mountain Brigade arrived there sent to the Merdani sector. They just passed by us. We gave them escorts, and they proceeded toward Merdani village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please use the same map you used a while ago. This is the map the scale of which is 1:50000. Can you put an arrow in the direction where this unit of the 303rd Brigade went to.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Kindly put a circle above the arrow and put number 303 within that circle.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know what the task of that unit was, of the unit that was sent to Merdani village? What was its mission?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Merdani had been shelled, and according to the information that we had from the population that had fled the village, there were two attempts to launch infantry attacks. These two attempts failed. And I was aware of the task of this unit because their commander told me that they had been sent by the corps pursuant to our information to provide security for Merdani village, because it was not known at the time whether any new infantry attacks would be attempted. We didn't know what units were available in Merdani village because they belonged to the Municipal Staff of Kacuni. So their exclusive task was to provide security for Merdani village, and within that scope they were also to provide security for the area behind Lasva local commune. If Merdani were protected and remained free, that meant that part of the territory bordering on our local community would also remain free.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that you tasked some of your troops to escort this unit. Why did you task troops from Lasva to go with these men?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: You mean to Merdani?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. We asked them to show them the way and to put them in touch with the villagers of this village so that these people would be aware that reinforcement was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, did you find out whether there was any other unit or a part of any other unit had arrived in the general area of that region during that night or, in other words, in the area that was covered by your unit?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of the 2nd Anti-Sabotage Detachment we saw the arrival of another unit from the 317 Mountain Brigade. This unit was billeted in the school in Janjici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to mark the place where that unit, the mortar battery, was billeted, and mark it with letters MB, which will show us that this was the place where the mortar battery was billeted.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. On line 23, page 34, the number is wrong. It says 317, and the witness said that it was the 17th Krajina Brigade, the 17th Brigade, that is. That is what --

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: 317 Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, tell me, please, do you know who the commander of this company of the 7th Muslim Brigade was, the one that was at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: The commander was Elvedin Camdzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time during that night between the 25th and the 26th or in the morning of 26th January that you had a conversation with Mr. Camdzic, and did he tell you on that occasion whether he had a certain mission or task?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a conversation with him during the night, and he told me why they were there. Their goal was to provide security for the Lasva crossroads and control the territory of Lasva local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you said there was a mortar battery of the 17th Brigade and the company of a 303rd Brigade there. This company of the 17th Brigade and the company of the 303rd Brigade, did they at any point in time on the 25th or on the 26th January enter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, please. In the transcript he said 317th. You are referring to that brigade as the 17th. He said the 317. Can we please be clear on this. When you're talking about the mortar company, was that a company of the 317th or the 17th brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say the 317th, but if that was not its name, then I may have been mistaken. I cannot guarantee what its name was. I don't know whether it was the 17th or the 317th, but it seems to me that it was the 317th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said 317th. Don't make him say 17th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I was not reading the transcript, and I might have overheard what the witness said. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the mortar battery that was billeted in Janjici, was there any other mortar battery present in Janjici; in other words, in the Janjici school?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. That battery was the only one there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, this battery or the troops of the 303rd which were moving towards Merdani, did they at any point in time on the 25th or the 26th of January enter the area of Lasva local commune or the territory of Dusina village?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. The troops did not enter Lasva because that was not their task. They did not engage in combat in the territory of this local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In reply to my question, you've told us that you had a conversation with the commander of the company of the 7th Muslim Brigade, Mr. Camdzic. In that conversation, did he tell you whether his task was to engage in combat in that area?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. As I've already told you, he told me that their exclusive task was to provide security for the Lasva crossroads and to secure the territory of Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Commander Camdzic ask for your assistance in any shape or form? Do you know whether his company, on the morning of the 26th, set off to a certain area? If that is the case, did you know what direction they went in?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: When combat started in Busovaca, and this reflected on the relationship within our local commune, whatever was going on in Busovaca had an immediate ripple effect on our local commune, it was to be expected that if Merdani were to fall or if the HVO came to the border area with Busovaca, the situation would no longer be certain and clear for us. He told me that in addition to providing security for the Lasva crossroads, he would take a platoon of men and start patrolling the area of Lasva local commune on that morning. He told me that he would go to reconnoiter and control the territory with some of his troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Awhile ago you told us that they had arrived a few days earlier. Did these men know anything about this area? Were they familiar with the territory?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They had been there for a week on the 26th of January. They were not familiar with the territory of the local commune. Up to that main -- up to that date, no member of the 7th Brigade had ever set foot in that local commune. They stayed at the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In light of the fact and given the fact that you were the deputy commander of an Anti-Sabotage Detachment, did Commander Camdzic ask you to provide him with certain assistance? Did you provide him with any assistance with the execution of his task?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I informed the commander with the situation as it was in the local commune. I told him that the HVO controlled the entire road from this checkpoint number 1 throughout the entire local commune and that it would not be advisable, if they were to control the territory, to take this road, because they could bump into them. The two groups did not know each other, and it could have ended up in undesirable consequences. That's why we instructed them to take a different road from their command post via some fields called Crna, for a simple reason: We wanted them to avoid bumping into the troops of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you have just told us, could you please draw that on the other map, on the 1:25000 map, and can you show the direction that the -- this platoon was supposed to go to, this platoon of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As I've already told you that these people were not familiar with the area, that's why I believe that I gave them two men from our detachment to show them and explain certain things to them. We gave them two of our men to take them by different routes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please take the other map, the map the scale of which is 1:25000 and use the marker to mark the route that they were supposed to follow.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I have that map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark the road that you suggested that they take.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: That would be that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Put an arrow from the set-off point towards the place where they were headed.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you in the morning of 26 January?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I was at the Lasva crossroads, in the house where the command of the 7th Muslim Brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you put a circle above this arrow that you have just drawn, and can you put letters "CS, 7th Muslim Brigade," or can you just put "7th Muslim Brigade."

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in the course of that day? Did there come a time when you received certain information from the field?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: On that morning -- now we know what happened, what incidents took place and what the consequences of those incidents were. The company commander said that he would accompany that platoon in controlling the territory of the local commune. His goal was to try and establish contact with the HVO, and the ultimate goal was to establish joint control of that road. It was to be expected that what had happened in Busovaca might have an impact on our local commune. And secondly, whenever there is an armed conflict, there is a realistic danger that some of the population would be injured. And the only way out would have been through Dusina. They would not have been able to use that road if we were not able to establish control of that road. So the goal was to control the local commune, to establish cooperation with members of the HVO in order to establish the joint control of the road, because we always said that regardless of what was going on around us in Busovaca, Vitez, and Zenica, and regardless of who was engaged in the war, that this should not reflect on us, and that is why we wanted to avoid being dragged into any conflict ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After a certain time in the course of the day, did you learn whether this unit reached the lines that they were supposed to secure or did something else happen?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: All this time I was at the command at the crossroads. A couple of hours later, a group of men of the 7th Muslim Brigade returned, and they had up to five or six captured members of the HVO. I asked them what had happened as soon as I saw these captured soldiers. I was certain that something bad had happened. And they told me that when they had arrived at Brdo hamlet, in that hamlet there were three or four houses inhabited by Bosniaks, and the rest of the houses were empty because the population had moved out to Zenica. And there were also three or four Croat families residing there. When they reached this hamlet called Brdo, they were -- they went behind somebody's house, somebody opened fire on them, and I believe that Elvedin Camdzic was hit in the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please make a circle around the place where you were told that fire had been opened on the company commander, and can you mark this place with a letter B, because I believe the name of that place is Brdo.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to what happened next?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: After that, a man called Softic ran up to the company commander to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. help him as he was falling down. As he was running towards him -- I was not an eyewitness so I can't tell you whether this was true or not -- at that moment while he was running up to the commander, he was also hit, and he died on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened next according to the information that you received?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: According to the information that I received from them, when the company commander and Softic were killed, there was an open fighting. The men were scared. Fire was opened on both sides. How did this conflict develop? I don't know, because I did not receive any precise information to that effect, but this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, when these men were setting off for this combat task, did they ever tell you that this was supposed to be an attack?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. There was no mention of any attack. They said that they were going to control the territory of the local commune in order to establish control over the road leading through Dusina. There was no mention of any attack of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, on that day, were you aware of the fact that the 17th Krajina Brigade and the 303rd Brigade had carried out an attack on the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. I've just told you that these two brigades were not engaged in combat in the territory of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, in the course of the day, did you notice any other events taking place in the local commune of Lasva? If that is the case, what do you know about these events? What happened later on?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I don't know what the course of the combat was. I was not an eyewitness. I was not in the area. I only know that during the day, in the afternoon hours, the civilian population and members of the Croatian Defence Council started arriving in the office of the local commune and in the school building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who provided security for the school and for the population that had arrived?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: The arrival took place in the afternoon, after 3.00 in the afternoon. All the population arrived; women, children, the elderly, and members of the Croatian Defence Council. I believe that they all came, some of them in uniform, some of them had already changed into civilian clothes. Later on, I heard that the fighting took place in the Vranjaca elevation, mount elevation until the afternoon hours. And once the HVO had realised that they didn't stand a chance, they withdrew into Donja Visnjica village. Some of them withdrew into Rajici. And when they realised that the civilian population was leaving their houses, they decided to join them. Some of them had arms, but they abandoned their arms en route. Some, however, brought their arms to the office of the local commune and left their arms there. Then they all proceeded towards the school where they were accommodated. There none of the members of the HVO had arms, so they could move freely, and they did indeed move freely from Brdo via Donja Visnjica, Kegelj, and Rajici, and they all arrived in the school. How they were organised, I wouldn't know. They carried arms, but there were -- there was no more shooting. They left their arms and they were all accommodated in the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that people were coming from Donja Visnjica and other locations. Did you see the people arriving? Were those people captured and taken in, or did they come of their own free will to the school area?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As the shooting could no longer be heard at the Lasva crossroads where I was, in the afternoon I, too, headed towards the village. I reached the school, because I had the keys of the school. When I was told that the people were coming, I opened the school so that they could be put up there. I didn't see a single member of the 7th Muslim or any other soldier leading them as if they were detainees nor that they were mistreated. They came there of their own free will, and they were put up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that after a few hours, in the morning five or six HVO soldiers were taken in. Tell me where they were put up.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They were brought to the headquarters of the 7th Muslim company at the Lasva crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn that day whether the fighting led to any consequences or, rather, whether there were casualties? Were there any dead or wounded?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: When a number of soldiers of the 7th Muslim reached the Lasva crossroads with the captured members of the HVO, I heard from them that two of our soldiers had been killed, Camdzic and Softic, that the fighting continued, though they had not been planned at all, and that there were other dead. I didn't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Barucija, at that point in time, were you in contact with Municipal Staff headquarters or with the 3rd Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. We had no communication with them. The only way to contact them was by telephone when they were working. However, on most occasions, there was no electricity in the local commune, so you couldn't call outside the building. So the only contact we had was by telephone, when that was possible, and directly. So that the Municipal Staff could not hear from us any report from the 7th Muslim. I know they did have some communication of their own, but that was not within my competencies. It was a unit that was resubordinated to the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence, and it was not up to me to interfere with what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My friends are telling me that the interpretation is not clear enough, so I'm going to repeat the question. Were you in communication with the Municipal Staff? Did you send them any information on that day?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: We were not in communication with the Municipal Staff, and we did not send them any reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether a company of the 7th Muslim had any communication with them, and do you know whether they sent any information?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I do know that they had some means of communication. Now, whether they sent information or report and to whom, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any authority over that company of the 7th Muslim Brigade or, rather, do you know to whom it was resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: We had no authority over them because they were resubordinated to the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, on that day, did you see, in addition to the soldiers that had been detained and the civilians who were coming and were put up in the school, were wounded people being brought in, and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: There were wounded on both sides. I think there were two to three army members that were wounded, and as many members of the HVO. I don't know whether anybody informed the medical unit of the corps, or did the corps, knowing that there had been some fighting, assume that there would be wounded and they sent a medical unit to take care of all the wounded, soldiers belonging both to the army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said a moment ago, Mr. Barucija, that you had heard that there had been casualties on both sides, did you learn that day or the following day what happened to the bodies of those killed?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I heard that the next day - and this was the 27th of January - that the bodies of the dead members of the army and the HVO were driven away by the Civil Defence to the mortuary of the Zenica hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the information that there had been dead on both sides, did you that day or the following days hear from anyone at all, members of the army, of the 7th Muslim, or from Croat citizens that the death of those persons had occurred due to some other reasons?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. All the information I had from all sources was that these people had been killed in direct clashes after the killing of Camdzic and Softic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, in your anti-sabotage unit, was there a police unit or some kind of investigating body that could perhaps check out those reports?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. Our Anti-Sabotage Detachment did not conduct any investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Barucija, after those events in the area of your local commune, and more specifically in the area of Dusina, did any kind of commission come? And if they did, tell us why.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As the territory of the local commune was reattached to the 7th Muslim Brigade after these events, from the company headquarters which was at the Lasva crossroads, I went to the command of the 2nd Anti-Sabotage Detachment, which was headquartered in Zenica. Two or three days later, with a couple of men, I went to Lasva again, I visited my family, and we went to Dusina to see, once everything had calmed down, the wounded had been taken care of, the dead had been transported to the mortuary, that we visit the village and try and collect more information. While we touring the village of Kegelj, I think it was deputy corps commander Dzemal Merdan who arrived. Then there was the commander of the HVO, I don't know his name; a representative of UNPROFOR; and an interpreter who was with them, the daughter of Jozo Kegelj, an inhabitant of the hamlet of Kegelji. We were introduced there. They saw that I too was some sort of military commander, and they told me that they had information that there had been a conflict there and that there had been slaughter, a massacre, and that the village had been set on fire, et cetera, et cetera. But they were able to see for themselves. We told them that the fighting started in such-and-such a way, that so many people had been killed, but that the village had not been burnt down. I think there were two houses whose roofs had been burnt. And after those conflicts, members of the HVO from Busovaca had shelled the local commune, and two shells fell on their houses, and that is how the roofs were destroyed. Those shells were fired at random throughout the territory of the local commune. They even reached the other bank of the Bosna River. The deputy commander had no information about what the HVO representative claimed, that there had been a massacre. He just said that there had been so many dead in an armed conflict, and they were able to see for themselves that the village had not been burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Barucija, when did you hear for the first time some different reports that were launched by the HVO or the Herceg-Bosna TV that described the situation in a different way from what you have told us?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: We received various reports from various sources, and we knew that some information was true but that there was also total disinformation, false information. And none of the people I met with among the soldiers or the inhabitants or even the Croats that we would see later, and we were on very good neighbours in the past, and nobody could understand why this had happened and how, but nobody mentioned a crime. They just said that what happened, happened, but nobody mentioned any crimes, nor did I have any such information. The first time I heard reports of that kind was that the Croatian propaganda was claiming a war crime of large proportions in October 1993. My brother's daughter lived in Busovaca, and she couldn't leave until October 1993. And when she came to Zenica, she told me that on television - I don't know whether it was Kiseljak television or Croatian television from the Republic of Croatia - anyway, that she had heard on television reports about that event to the effect that the Croatian population in Lasva had been massacred, that there were tens of killed civilians, women, and children, burnt houses, and the exodus of the Croats, and that Zeljko Cvijanovic had named me personally, showing a bayonet he would use to punish me for what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Barucija, do you know what was the attitude of civilian and military authorities regarding the protection of property after those events?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: After those events, it was normal to expect possible attacks on the local commune. So I think that the command of the 7th Muslim stayed there for a few more days, after which they withdrew, and the zone of responsibility was again taken over by the 2nd Anti-Sabotage Detachment. Behind the village of Dusina we formed a line in case of an attack so as to protect the local commune in such an event, but it never came about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were the civilian authorities operating at the time and taking measures to protect the Croatian population and the property of those who had left the local commune? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I do know that elements from the local commune, primarily through the Civil Defence forces, joined in clearing up the ground, in taking care of the population, in giving them some moral support, telling them that what had happened had happened due to force of circumstances but not due to anyone's intentions. The Civil Defence took care of the population, of the livestock, because some Croats had started leaving the territory. Some were going to Zenica, some to Busovaca, but some also stayed. I think in March and April, they were still there. But as for those who left, their livestock was taken care of as well as their abandoned property, because one could expect some looting to take place. And I know that the Civil Defence organised the collection of belongings from the abandoned houses, and these belongings were put in the school again, which was not working because of the war, and if they did not return, and they didn't return, then these belongings were distributed, with receipts, to refugees who were coming later in waves from Busovaca and other places. So the civilian authorities took care of the villages, their livestock and their belongings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Barucija. Would you please look at both maps that you have before you and which you marked at my request. Would you please sign those two maps and date them.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness, and I should like to tender these two maps into evidence as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Regarding the admission of the maps, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we don't have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we have two maps. Two numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They will be admitted under the Exhibit numbers as follows: The first map indicated by the witness, DH347. The map which indicates four points. And the second map marked by the witness will be admitted as DH348, with five -- five checkpoints and their locations marked on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The other Defence team for their questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the time period of the indictment for Mr. Kubura begins with the 1st of April, so we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have a few questions. If I can have a moment to put a little podium onto my desk. One second, please. Your Honours, I'll -- with your leave, I'll be using later just two exhibits with this witness. These will be P530 and P131, and I will have a number copies for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Barucija.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to discuss a few issues with you in the next hour and a half, perhaps a little bit more, and I hope you can help us in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. clarifying these things. Let me ask you first, you said you were the director of the elementary school in Janjici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this Janjici, that's the same village or small town which is up on the River Bosna, and I think you marked it as the location of the mortar unit. That's the same village or little city?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you weren't really the schoolmaster or director of the school in Lasva; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. I was director of that school too. The central school is in Janjici, and in our educational system, there are regional classes. And the school in Lasva belonged to the school in Janjici, so it was all one entity, one school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I see. So you were also in charge of the school in Lasva?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's why you had the key on the afternoon of the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I heard carefully to what you were testifying this morning, and the way I understand it, you weren't really an eyewitness to what was happening in the course, certainly, of the 26th of January, in the morning, around the hill -- or the village of Brdo. You weren't present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: That is correct; I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So everything that was reported to you was observed, witnessed, perhaps told by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the people who reported, you understand, were the people from that unit from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade which was stationed with you at the confluence of the Lasva and the Bosna River; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They were members of the 7th Muslim Brigade and two members of our detachment who were attached to them to assist them. So I learnt from both of these the information about the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
