utterances.text: So are you saying that also members of your -- of the 2nd Detachment was at the Brdo village together with the people from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. In those days, members of our detachment were not in the territory of the local commune but just at the confluence we had two or three of our members to assist them, to explain things to them. It wasn't a military unit, just two or three men who acted as guides for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I was only interested in the information that you received on the morning of the 26th of January about the events in Brdo. That information you received exclusively from members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: From members of the 7th Muslim Brigade and two members of our own detachment who went with them as guides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I see. Now I understand it.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: The information I received were identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the two members of the two escorts who went with the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I think one was Bulut Mujo, and I don't remember who the other one was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who gave you the information mainly about these -- the killing of the company commander? I think his name is Mr. Camdzic. Was it the two members from your unit or was it the members of the 7th Muslim Brigade? Do you remember that? It's a long time ago, of course.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: The information about the killing and the events following the killing reached me from members of the 7th Muslim Brigade and our two members; from both of them. Now, who the members of the 7th Muslim Brigade were, I really don't know. I didn't know a single one of them by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who had more information to give you, the people from your unit, your two escorts, or the other people, the other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: The same. What one set said, the others did as well; not more, not less. That they arrived at the village, upon arriving at the village, a shot was fired, killing Camdzic. After that, Softic was killed, and that's when the fighting started. That is what both said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did they also tell you about the murder of Mr. Zvonko Rajic?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So they didn't tell you the circumstances of how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They did not. I heard about Zvonko Rajic's killing the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I don't know. One of the locals when I came in the afternoon to open the school. One of the local people, I really don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: A Muslim local or a Croat local?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They told me that Zvonko Rajic had been killed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did they tell you --

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They asked me whether I had heard that Zvonko had been killed. I said I hadn't, and they said it appears that he has been killed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did they give you the circumstances of how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They didn't, and I think they couldn't, because those, they were locals who were in Lasva, and the events were at Dusina. So they just heard, probably by telephone. I don't know how. So they didn't speak about the details, nor could they know about the details. If they did know, they could have only heard from others the way I heard from others, because we were not witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned they may have or probably heard by telephone. So the telephones were working at that time on that day?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They were always working within the local commune regardless of whether there was electricity or not. Locally. But if there is no electricity, then you could not communicate beyond Lasva, nor could Lasva be reached. But within Lasva, the telephone was functioning always.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about a number of persons, and you may know them or not. Just tell me, please: Do you know a person called Serif Patkovic?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Personally, no, but I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I heard that he was commander. What exactly he was at that time, I think he was battalion commander and, later, commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And battalion commander means commander of a battalion within the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And would that be his position in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I think so. I'm not sure, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, on the 26th of January, you know, you were at the confluence of those rivers, in the morning at least, talking to members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. Did you see Serif Patkovic on that day?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I saw him in the afternoon. He came to Lasva in front of the school when almost all the Croatian population had reached the school. So I saw him sometime around 4.00 p.m. in front of the school. I hadn't seen him before that in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you talk to him when you saw him in the afternoon in front of the school?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I did. We introduced one another. I told him that I was the school principal, I also told him what my position was in the 2nd Anti-Sabotage Detachment, and that I had come to unlock the door of the school so that the population could be put up there. That was the first time that we met. And I never saw Patkovic again. I have never seen him before that nor after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sorry, did he ask you to open the school, or why did you open the school?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. I told him that I had come to open the school because the civilian population was arriving and we should house them there. He didn't ask for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did he say something to you?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I think he said, "That's fine. That was a good thing you did." I think something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see him entering the school?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No, he didn't enter the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: For how long were you around at that school? I believe you came around 4.00, but please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Around 4.00. I think that was the time when the people started arriving. Among them there were five soldiers of the HVO, some in uniform, some in civilian clothes. They were being put up in the school. I stayed there, I think, until around 6.00 p.m., primarily to make sure that all the people are put up and that they're okay. I didn't fear any reprisals, but still I was their neighbour. And they would come there often as parents to attend parents' meetings. They would come to my home, we socialised. I wanted to make sure that they were all right and that I could then leave. Patkovic did not enter the school, and the school was secured by a squad, I think from the 1st Sabotage Detachment. Soldiers of the 7th Muslim Brigade were not in the school at the time, nor did they enter the school premises at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a difference in uniforms between the members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade and the anti-sabotage detachments? Could you distinguish which one was which?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I believe that the colours differed. Those were camouflage uniforms with the insignia of the BiH army. It was already dark, however, I had spent time with them during the day in the command, and I didn't see anything special about them. I don't know whether they were better equipped than our detachment. I think that their boots were better, they had gloves; but those were the only differences that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just going back to something you just told us, that the squad of the 1st Anti-Sabotage Detachment was guarding these HVO soldiers. How big was the squad?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: It was a small unit with some seven to ten men altogether. Their task was to secure the school in order to prevent any incidents from taking place where these people were there. It was war. War operations were taking place. It would not have been advisable to keep those hundred men, women, and children there without any security.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So there were about a hundred men and women there at the school?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: There were women, children. The entire population, regardless of their age.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But only Croats.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Only Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it was not just civilians but also I believe you mentioned five HVO soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: There were civilians and most of the HVO members. Some 30 of them were in uniform, and the rest of them had already changed into civilian clothes. After combat, they went back home, they put on civilian clothes and joined the rest. They were all there. Most of them were in uniform, but they were not afraid to come to the school. And we knew all of them. They were all our neighbours, so we knew that even those who wore civilian clothes were members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So why, then, did they need to be guarded by a squad from the anti-sabotage detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: It was just a precaution. It was already dark. It was a measure of precaution. We never thought that anything tragic might occur. This is just how things are done in the army. Wherever there is a group, a large group of people, those people have to be guarded. Somebody could have just walked in with a hand grenade and blown the place up. There were drunk people around, there were lunatics around, so we had to have some precaution measures in order to prevent something unforeseen happen and something that an individual could have caused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go back to the squad. Who was the -- and I believe you said the squad was part of the 1st Detachment of the anti- -- yes, 1st Detachment, and I believe you were the commander of the 2nd Detachment. Now, who was the commander of the 1st Anti-Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: The commander of that detachment was Zajko Kozlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was he present that evening?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many much squads does an anti-sabotage detachment have?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: It consists of three squads, and every squad has three platoons. One squad has anything between eight and hundred men. Every squad has three platoons, and every platoon has smaller units, three such units consisting of eight to ten people. So three small units are a platoon, three platoons are a squad, three squads are a company. Kozlic Zajko was the commander, he must have given some tasks to the staff, and the staff has issued an order to us. There were between eight and ten people. Their commander brought them. They provided security for the school in order to prevent anything unforeseeable happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if one of the persons there, one of the HVO soldiers, tried to leave because he knew a friend in the area who has sort of house he could stay, would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Are you referring only to HVO members or any Croat citizen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Everybody there. If anybody would have left -- would have wanted to leave, because probably not too much fun to stay in a cramped classroom, would he or she be allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They were there of their own will. I don't know how they organised themselves to get there, whose idea it was. In any case, they all arrived of their own will, both the civilians and HVO members. And they could go wherever they wanted, because until that day, we socialised, we visited each other. Around 1800 hours, I left the school. I heard that they stayed in the school for three or four hours. It was winter, it was cold, they didn't have any food there. It was nobody's goal to kept them during the night. They were not captives. They just came there of their own will, feeling that they would be safer there than in the village. After those three or four hours, they all left the school. Some of them went back home, and some stayed with their Muslim neighbours. All the while when they were in the school, a Croatian family whom I socialised with were in my apartment. They were not in the school, they were in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, who told you that they were there on their free will?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I suppose that they came of their own will or they organised themselves freely. I only know that they came. I know that Faruk Barucija and Ivica Kristo, who were really, really good friends, one's a Muslim and the other is a Croat, the two of them went from one house to another, inviting people to come to the school. They all listened to them and nothing ever happened to them on the way to the school or in the school. If they hadn't trusted me, if they hadn't been sure that the school would be a safe place for them, they would not have come. If the members of the HVO felt safe, then of course you must understand that they all felt safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I asked you before whether anybody would be allowed to leave, and I believe you said yes. Now, asking specifically about the HVO soldiers, people, were they also, in your opinion, allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: If somebody had asked me, I would say yes, because they all came of their own free will. They were not forced to go there. If somebody had asked me whether they were free to go home that very moment, I would have said yes, but I would have also told them not to do that because they wouldn't be safe there. It was dark, it was night, anything could have happened. But as I say, if anybody had asked me, I would have said yes, they would have been free to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, were they all together, the civilians and the HVO, or were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they in two or perhaps more different classrooms, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: When they entered the school, they could not all fit in one classroom. Those classrooms are very small. The surface of those classrooms is 37 to 38 square metres. And as they were entering those two classrooms, they organised themselves. All civilians entered one classroom, and members of the HVO entered the other classroom. They did it again of their own initiative. As they were entering the school, that's how they sort of divided themselves into two different groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Like magic, coming in, and so the civilians, very disciplined, left and to the right. That's what it looked like to you, very disciplined. The people, you know, without any orders given, one group into one classroom and the other one into the other one. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: That's how they entered. That's how they organised themselves. I don't know if there was anybody at the entrance telling them what to do, whether there was any member of security who told them what to do and where to go, I don't know that. I only know that that's how they were divided, that's how they were organised. If -- even if they had been in one room, you could see who members of the HVO were, because they wore uniforms. Most of them were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see, while you were there in those two hours from, I believe, 4.00 to 6.00, did you see any mistreatment of the HVO soldiers or perhaps civilians?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. There was absolutely no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did somebody tell you about mistreatment happening in one of the classrooms or outside?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. No. I never heard of any such thing. In the course of those few hours, this certainly didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, perhaps you can assist us with a few names. Can you tell us names of HVO soldiers you saw being kept at the school on that evening, 26th of January, 1993? Whom did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They were all there, all of them. There were no exceptions. They were all there. I knew them as if we had lived in one house. The Rajics, the Kristos, the Kegeljs, the Radoses. All of those family names were present, were represented. So all the people that lived in those villages were there. I could give you all the names and family names, but if I tell you they were all there, I don't see the need for me to tell them their individual names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Did you talk to them, any of them?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I felt very awkward in such a situation. I believe you can imagine. We were neighbours, there were casualties on both sides. There were no casualties amongst Bosniaks from Lasva, but there were casualties amongst Croats. They arrived in the school. They did experience some degree of fear, and I really feel very, very awkward and embarrassed to meet them or to talk to them in light of the relations that we had had in the past. I did exchange a few words with somebody - I don't remember who it was - and their comment was, Look what has happened to us. All this time we were saying, Let's not do this, who needed this? and still this happened. And I left the classroom, because the circumstances were very difficult for me. It is not because I felt any hostility towards them. The circumstances were such as they were, and we found ourselves in those circumstances without any need for us to face such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I believe you mentioned one of the citizens of that village before, Zeljko Cvijanovic. Do you remember this person?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, was he one of the persons you saw in the school?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I believe so. I cannot be sure of that, but I should think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What were you wearing on that day, by the way?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform and a heavy overcoat. I did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the other members of the -- you know, the squad which was guarding the school, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Of course they were. How would the troops provide security without arms?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, would you be surprised to hear that people in the classrooms were mistreated that night?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I would. I would, because according to the information that I have, nobody was mistreated. I never heard any such thing from anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you about another name. Velid Subotic. Do you know such a person?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. I've never heard the name before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: He also goes by the nickname of Geler.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I've heard of Geler. Geler is a shell fragment. When a shell explodes, that's a geler. I did hear people mentioning Geler as somebody who did participate in combat. That was the context, but who the man was, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: He had a very distinctive feature; he had a glass eye.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, on that day did you see him or did you hear that he was in the area?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: If you don't know a person, how can you say that you saw him? I may have seen him, but I didn't know that it was him. Velimir Subotic you said. I don't know. I've never heard of anybody called Velimir Subotic. I did hear people mentioning somebody called Geler, but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember what the people were talking about Geler, and only as it relates to the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object. The witness has not said anything about what Geler did on the 26th of January, so the question is not grounded in any of the answers provided by the witness so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution doesn't ask what Geler did on the 26th. The witness said that he did hear people mentioning Geler, and the Prosecution didn't ask the witness what Geler did on the 26th. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I can repeat, Witness. You said that -- yes. People -- you heard people talking about him. I'm just merely asking whether you heard people talking about him having a certain involvement in the events of the 26th of January, 1993. You gave us a lot of hearsay today, so perhaps you have also heard something about Mr. Geler.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I have told you that I don't know Velid Subotic. When you said that he also goes by the name Geler, I told you that I heard of somebody referred to as Geler but I don't know who that person is or what he did. I've heard of Geler. Whether that was Velimir Subotic or not, I don't know, and I don't know what Geler did; I only heard that Geler existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me show you - with your leave, Mr. President - a document, a combat report from one of these anti-sabotage detachments, and it's Exhibit P530. Now, if you could just look at the -- these two pages, just quickly familiarise yourself, see the person who signed it. I believe you mentioned his name already, but if you can tell the Trial Chamber who the person is who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: The person who signed is Zajko Kozlic, commander of the 1st Anti-Sabotage Detachment. I don't know whether this is his authentic signature. I cannot be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this is a combat report pertaining to the events we are talking around, or it appears to be about the events we are talking about, and I would like -- you are mentioned twice in this document, so perhaps you could enlighten us as to what your role was at that day. Now, the second paragraph, starting with "On 28th January 1993, around 13 hours," talks about the involvement of the 2nd PDO, that's the Anti-Sabotage Detachment. Then it goes on. In the middle we see that commander Serif Patkovic coordinated the whole operation. That's what it says here. And then it goes on, and I would like to -- to read it out to you, and perhaps you can follow us. It says: "The 2nd PDO Operations Officer Hazim Barucija rejected the surrender and organised the reorganisation of the HVO forces with our platoon. It was agreed that all weapons be placed in a pile outside Zvonko Rajic's house and that they proceed towards the school in Lasva with their arms in the air." And then it goes on and talks about the -- that's the next paragraph, the separations between civilians and soldiers, that they are placed in different rooms in the school, that the soldiers were searched, operation lasting between 4.00, that's when you arrived at the school, and 7.00. A squad arrived, and we heard that from you as well, and so on. And then it mentions you again. That's the next paragraph, and I quote: "From 1900 to 2030 hours, we held them in classrooms, and after receiving approval from the 2nd PDO operations officer - that's the same function attributed to you in the paragraph above, "turned them over to the company commander Salih Heco, or Heco, to guard them." Now, you having been on -- present at that day, perhaps you can tell us how you see these comments or this report made by the commander of the 1st Anti-Sabotage Detachment. And perhaps I should add you have seen -- he talks about 28th of January, 1993, and perhaps you have an opinion about the date as well, the report being drafted on 22nd February 1993, a month, almost, after the events. Now, can you tell us what your observations are on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I observe the time. I'm entirely in your hands. Perhaps the witness would like to read it over during the break. It's entirely up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, maybe it would be best for you to take the time to read this document during the break. It is half past twelve. We're going to resume in 25 minutes, and I would like to remind everybody that we continue until quarter to two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before continuing, regarding the time. The Defence used one hour, forty minutes, whereas originally one hour was planned. Theoretically, the Prosecution has one hour forty, which means that will take us on to Monday. If the Prosecution wishes to use the same amount of time, they may. The Chamber has also some questions to put to the witness. There will be a re-examination. So apparently it is quite possible, sir, that you will be staying until Monday. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No, I won't be using all my name. I think it would be preferable if Mr. Barucija could go home over the weekend. I can only just shorten my cross-examination and perhaps that leaves time for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Barucija, I hope you still could have a good break, but at the same time, did you have a chance to familiarise yourself with this document?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I have read this combat report during the break, and I can say the following: There's a factual error in the date. So it isn't the 28th of January but the 26th. This combat report was written a month after the event. They are usually written immediately after certain events, so it's a bit strange that so much time had elapsed, but that doesn't matter. What the commander of the 1st Anti-Sabotage Detachment says, that he received orders from the Territorial Defence Staff, he probably did. I don't know what orders he received. I know that we saw one another in Lasva between 3.00 and 4.00 in the afternoon, that he told me that they had been given certain assignments, and I told him, on the basis of the information that we had, that the population had been informed and that they were coming to the school, and there was no need to implement those assignments they had been given, and those were to take positions in the Lasva River valley and to encircle villages of Donja Visnjica and others. There was no need to do this because the Croatian population was already coming to the school. On the other hand, MOS and other units are referred to. They are not MOS but a company of the 7th Muslim Brigade who had stayed there, and they also started arriving sometime after 4.00. My name is mentioned here. I don't know what he meant. "The operations officer from the 2nd Anti-Sabotage Detachment unit rejected this surrender and organised with our platoon the realisation of the HVO forces." I really don't know what this means. Probably the detachment commander was given these assignments, but there was no need to implement or realise those tasks except for securing the school once all the people had arrived. So perhaps could you explain to me what this means in this sentence where my name is mentioned? I don't know what I wanted to organise regarding the realisation of the HVO forces with our platoon. I don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just the term in the second paragraph in the middle, the term "the civilians surrendered," "surrendered to the units in Lasva." That doesn't suggest that they came, as you repeatedly said, at their free will. And I take it this commander who wrote this report has more information about that than you who has not, as you said, spoken to these people.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they did not come by force but of their own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you, on the second page of this document, just the second sentence to last. It says: "The platoon returned to Bistricak base on 31st of January, 1993." Can you tell us where this base, the Bistricak base of the Anti-Sabotage Detachment was?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: The 1st Anti-Sabotage Detachment covered the area of responsibility of the local commune of Nemila -- Nemila, which is quite a large area covering more than ten villages, and Bistricak is one of those villages in the Nemila local commune, which is to the north. You can see it on the map. Upstream -- no, sorry, downstream. You will see Nemila. That was the area of responsibility of the 1st Anti-Sabotage Detachment and their base was in Bistricak. Now, what they were doing on the 31st of January, I don't know. They only spent that one night in Lasva and then they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, how close to Lasva, Lasva village, is Bistricak?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: From Lasva to Zenica it's 16 kilometres, and from Zenica to Nemila I think 40 kilometres. From Nemila to Bistricak another 10 or so kilometres, so that would make it 50 to 60 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In what direction, north from Lasva?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: North, yes, north; downstream.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just a couple of points to clear up. This -- you told us that when you were at that confluence, the headquarters of the company from the 7th Muslim -- Mountain Muslim Brigade on the morning and the days before of the 26th of January, then these five HVO soldiers were captured and brought. Who were these people? Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: That happened on the 26th of January, after the conflict had started. I think one of them was Viktor Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the other ones?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I really don't know the names of the others. I can claim with certainty that Viktor Rajic was one of them. And there was five to six of them. After all, it was 12 years ago, so one forgets the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, apart from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, also the 303 Brigade, I guess. Now, how do you know that, first, the unit you were located with was from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade? Did somebody tell you? Did they have insignias? Did you know them Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. personally?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: They told me, and when I returned from Maglaj, as I passed through by train, because at the confluence of the Lasva and the Bosna, there's a railway bridge, and just below it is the house where our guards were housed and the company of the 7th Muslim. I saw people I didn't know, and when I got off the train, I was told by friends that because our people had gone to the front, that they were replaced by a company of the 7th Muslim Brigade who were securing the crossroads and everything else that we spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you were told by friends but not by these people from -- the soldiers from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: When I came from Maglaj and first went home, when from my home I went to the headquarters of the detachment, I was briefed on the whole situation, and I learnt in the headquarters and also from information I got at home that this was -- that these were members of the 7th Muslim Brigade who were a regular part of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the same question in relation to the 303 Brigade. How do you know those were the people, you know, which came -- the unit which came to help out in -- I think in Merdani? So how do you know that these people, these soldiers, were from the 303 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: When that unit arrived, I assume that in the corps command, they were told to report to us at the confluence, where we were, that they would be given two or three men to assist them, to take them to Merdani. And when they arrived, we asked them who they were, and they said that they were members of the Railway Battalion which was part of the 303rd Mountain Brigade. This is the ironworks company which had a battalion of its own which was part of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me briefly show you another document, the second document, P131. Now, you told us this morning that there was this unit, and I think you showed it on one of the exhibits, that came from the -- your position and passed -- passed along to the village of Brdo. And then I think that's the unit who came back with HVO soldiers. Now, looking at this document now, and this appears to be a report by the 7th Muslim Brigade, and it talks about that action, and the first sentence and the second one says that: "In the morning on that day, early morning hours, we captured elevation 852 above the village of Lasva," and then talks about who were -- was the unit involved, 2nd Company of 2nd Battalion, and later, we also see in the middle that, indeed as you told us, the commander, Elvedin Camdzic, was killed. Now, it appears from this document that in fact they didn't just pass by and went to the village of Brdo as you told us, but they got the elevation. It even talks about "captured" the elevation. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not at the elevation, nor was that their assignment. All the information I received from everybody else was that they set off from the headquarters and entered the village of Brdo. They didn't capture any elevation. I don't know why this report says this. My information is that they entered the village of Brdo after the killing, as I have already described. About reaching elevation 852 is something I have no knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you think Mr. Asim Koricic, who signed for the commander of that brigade, would have misled in an official report to the duty officer of the 3rd Corps about taking the dominant elevation of the Lasva area? Do you think he may have misled his commander?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. I can't say what he meant and what he wished. I'm just saying that my knowledge does not concur with this. Now, what his intentions were is something I can't comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And help us again with where your knowledge comes from.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: My knowledge comes from both members of the 7th Muslim Brigade who came after the conflict to the headquarters and from our own soldiers who went with them and after I arrived in the Lasva in the afternoon. As for this elevation and its feature and its capture, I heard nothing about it. Because there was no need to capture that elevation. Elevation 852, I think it is Crna. There's already a company of the Ironworks Battalion in Merdani village. Now, why it was written like this, I really don't know. I have no knowledge of the elevation being captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't want to enter into a military discussion, but do you think there is a military sense in capturing the highest elevation point in an area? You as deputy commander of the 2nd Anti-Sabotage Detachment, do you think there is a military sense in capturing the highest elevation of an area?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: A military reason may certainly exist, but just then there was no need, nor do I have any knowledge that that is what happened. Of course a capture of a certain elevation gives you a control and better view of a certain area, but at that point in time, this was not necessary, and I have no knowledge that it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just incidentally, did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I did my regular military service, but I was not an active-duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But did you leave with a rank?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. I served in the former JNA like any other citizen. I was a soldier. I graduated from the school of reserve officers and had the rank of reserve captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's briefly talk about this commission who said -- who came to -- I believe you said a couple of days after the events, to your area, and then they were talking about, I think, an UNPROFOR person was talking about slaughter, the way I understood you. Can you name us this UNPROFOR person with whom you had contacts?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I don't know that, who was present on behalf of UNPROFOR. I don't know who the commander of the HVO from Zenica was. I just know that there was the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, Dzemal Merdan. As for these other two persons, I never saw them before in my life and I really don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could you help us with his rank, the UNPROFOR person, the nationality? Sometimes that is something you could catch, rank and nationality, of the UNPROFOR --

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Now, were you ever interrogated, interviewed by a police or security or military person in relation to the events on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did somebody else -- are you aware whether somebody else from your unit, of which you were deputy commander, was answering questions in relation to any such investigations? Have you heard -- are you aware of anything?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one from our detachment, because our detachment did not have any assignments in that area at that time. So I have no such knowledge of any interrogations of members of our detachment or any kind of investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, you told us this morning that your area of responsibility, or the one of your detachment, was that area, Lasva and the other villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That was the area of responsibility of our detachment, but at the time that members of our detachment went to the front in Maglaj, the resubordinated company of the 7th Muslim Brigade to -- was resubordinated directly to the territorial staff, so they became fully responsible and competent for any subsequent actions. We couldn't command a company of the 7th Muslim Brigade because it was resubordinated to the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence to which we were subordinated as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: My last question is about Serif Patkovic, whom you have mentioned. Do you know what he's doing now, what his role, his function, his job is?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I have heard that he has a farm somewhere. Up until two years ago, he was in the Zenica-Doboj canton, minister for veterans affairs. But just now I don't think he is employed anywhere, but he has a farm of his own. That is what I heard. I don't really know. I saw the man only once in my life, on that day, at that time, and never again. We had no contacts or any activities after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now -- and that's really my last question. I apologise. You told us that you weren't aware of any mistreatments and that nobody had told you about that in relation to the people who were kept at the school. Now, after the events, after you left, I believe, at 8.00 that evening, did you ever talk to the local people, the Croats, who were kept at that school? Did you ever talk to them again?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I said that I left the school about 6.00 p.m., not 8.00 p.m., and according to what I know, the citizens stayed in the school up until about 9.00, and after that, they were released. All the civilians were released home or wherever they wanted to go. Of course I did later see those neighbours, Rajic Miroslav, for instance, who was a friend of mine. He was a member of the army, he was with us in the unit, and the man never told me that there had been any mistreatment in the school that evening. And as far as I know, they stayed there until 9.00 p.m., and they were released home. As for the HVO soldiers, they were taken to the KP Dom in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When did you talk to Miroslav Rajic for the first time after the events?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Maybe a couple of days after that, because I went to the headquarters and we had other assignments. So several days later, when we saw each other. Anyone, like Marko Rajic. We were good friends, we worked together in the local commune together as well. No one ever mentioned any kind of mistreatment in the school, absolutely never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where is Miroslav Rajic today?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I think that, with his family, he's in America.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Marko Rajic is in Lasva. He returned to Lasva, and he's living there to this day. So according to all the information I have, there was never any mistreatment in the school at all. Marko Rajic has returned and has been living in Lasva for several years, and he might be the closest person to those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I appreciate your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I would like to ask you a few small questions on the last part of your testimony, and that is your meeting with the commission a short time after the fighting on the 26th of January. You said -- you told us that you saw, when touring in the neighbourhood of Dusina, the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, Mr. Merdan, and you saw a person from UNPROFOR, an HVO commander, and an interpreter. And you mentioned the name of the interpreter, but I noticed that it was not reflected in the record, but I think I understood the name of the interpreter. Could you tell us who the interpreter was?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Milica Kegelj, the daughter of Jozo Kegelj, who lived in the hamlet of Kegelj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I had the impression -- I understood the name Kegelj also. Now, she has been here in December last year, almost a year ago, and she said that she returned to Dusina with a commission of UNPROFOR on the 11th of February. Could that be right? Could that be the date? Because you spoke about a few days after the events.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: It's possible. From this time distance, it could have been the beginning of February. I said a few days. It could be five or six or seven, but it wasn't a long time after the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The commission you saw was composed of these four persons, or were there other members of the commission present, or were there just three and the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, just the four of them; a representative of the army, of the HVO, of UNPROFOR, and the interpreter. It wasn't a real meeting. We were on the ground, doing our own things, and we happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You met them in the open field, so to speak. You were touring around, maybe on foot, maybe in a car, and suddenly you met them somewhere in the neighbourhood of Dusina? Where was it exactly, under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: We were reconnoitering the terrain because, not knowing how things would develop in Busovaca, we expected combat activities towards the Lasva commune. We formed a defence line behind Dusina towards Busovaca, and we were touring the area and we came across them. They didn't know about us, nor did we know about then.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And when you say "we," you imply the members of the 2nd Detachment, your anti-sabotage unit?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: How many of you were there at the moment?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I mean the associates that were with me; the company commander and his deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you were three, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you started to talk with them, or they invited you to talk, and they put you questions? Did you go anywhere or was it on the spot, or could you tell me some more details on how this interview or this conversation went?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: We didn't talk at length because we didn't know about them coming, nor did they know that there was someone up there. What their aim was, I don't know. I know that Milica Kegelj was pointing out her house, which had already been burned down by a shell coming from Busovaca. As they saw that I was wearing certain insignia which meant I was in the military, and I knew the deputy corps commander and I introduced myself, I said, Deputy, I am so-and-so. We have formed defence lines towards Busovaca, and that was it. We were just witnesses of the arrival of that commission independently of one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Was Milica Kegelj also present in the school on the 26th of January? Do you remember having seen her there?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I think not. I think she wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So it was the commission and the three of you, I suppose. There were no other persons present except the members of the commission, the interpreter, and you three, the three of your unit?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were the four of them. I with my associates, we were touring the lines, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You spoke about the HVO commander whose name you don't remember. Somewhere later in your testimony you spoke about an HVO representative, but I take it that these are the same person. There were no other members of the HVO present at the -- at the moment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Are you referring to the commission that arrived?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yeah. You spoke about the HVO commander and later on you spoke about the HVO representative. And just to be sure, to exclude any other possibilities, I ask you, is this the same person?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the same person. Whether he was the commander of the HVO in Zenica or his deputy or somebody else, I don't know. In any case, he was a member of the HVO from Zenica; the same person, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So it is the HVO commander who claims that there has been a massacre. Is that a proper conclusion, then? One of the members of the commission, the HVO commander, is telling you that there has been a massacre. Is that your testimony? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I heard this representative of the HVO or their commander, or whatever his position was, mentioning a massacre. He used the word "massacre," but nobody else. What the context was, I don't know. Later on, what I heard from the propaganda, they started talking about this massacre immediately after that day. We did not, however, have any information about the massacre. It was a regular combat operation, nothing else. And I've already said that my niece left Busovaca, what she saw on TV. Already a day later they reported about a terrible massacre having taken place, casualties among civilians, women, the whole village being torched. I suppose it was that context that he was mentioning the massacre in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this commission. You said the HVO commander claimed that there has been a massacre, and I wrote down - please correct me if I'm wrong - that the deputy commander, meaning Mr. Merdan, said there was no information about what the HVO commander claimed. Are these your words, and is this your recollection also?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So there was, so to speak -- there were, so to speak, two views. The HVO commander said there has been a massacre, and Mr. Merdan saying, "I have no information about a massacre." May interpreter -- may I understand the situation in these terms, or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, you may. According to the information that we had, the killings happened in the way I described them. I was not an eyewitness. I only heard about that. But in any case, all the killings happened during combat. On the other hand, the Croatian side, already on the 27th, started talking about a horrendous massacre and dozens of civilians having been massacred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... questioning. Was the UNPROFOR person the person who interviewed you or were the HVO commander and Mr. Merdan putting questions to you or did you just tell your story? How was the interview going? How was it conducted?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: We didn't spend any time with them. They came independently of us. They didn't know that we were there, we didn't know that they would arrive; we just bumped into them. I introduced myself, I told the deputy commander why we were there, that we were inspecting the combat positions, and then I heard a representative of the HVO speaking about massacre. Nobody asked us anything, and we did not continue to participate in any of the talks. It was not an organised meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how long the meeting took; a few minutes, more, or less?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: We spent maybe five or six minutes with them and then we proceeded, and they stayed there on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I noted down you said during your testimony, "We told them that the fighting started in such-and-such a way and that so many people had been killed but that the village had not burned." Was that the essence of what you said or did you add more detail?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that was mostly that. I was not in a position to speak about the facts objectively, because I was not an eyewitness to the incidents. I just interpreted to anybody who asked me about things the things that I had heard, the things that I had heard from others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And the same was true for your -- the other members of your detachment? They were not present at the events either; is that correct? You were all at the Lasva junction on the 26th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: What incident are you referring to, what event?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I think you heard from others on the 26th, or after, before you met the commission, was only that there had so many people been killed. I'm asking this because there are two stories. There is the Croatian story saying there has been a massacre, some people had been killed after fighting, and there is another story saying these people have all been killed during the battle. So you haven't been there, you can't tell us anything about that, but I want to make sure what exactly you said to this commission. Did you speculate about the circumstances? Did you say they were all killed in combat, or did you say, "I don't know about the circumstances," that kind of thing? Can you tell me anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I received information from various sources. According to all that, the killings happened in the way that I described. The information that I conveyed to the others who asked me about this incident was that our men and members of the HVO were killed in an armed conflict which followed the killings of Softic and Camdzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And between the 26th and the 11th of February, if it was that date, you didn't speak, I understood from what you answered to the Prosecutor, with someone of the family of Kegelj, for instance, or other Croats from Dusina?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any of them, because I believe that they left the village immediately, and nobody remained up there. And a few days later, the village was empty; there were no Kegeljs in the village. Some were still in Donja Visnjica and some were in Rajici. Kegelji was completely empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My final question then, to come back to what you said on the 26th. There are two possibilities. You either said to the commission so many persons have been killed on that day, or you said the same thing and you added, "I believe they were killed in combat." What did you say exactly, to make absolutely sure what you said, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any such questions and answers. If there were, I can't say for sure. If I had been asked and if I had answered, then I could only say that so many people on the two sides were killed. I never heard anybody conveying to me any information about the killings or that I conveyed to anybody such information, because nobody ever spoke to me about murders, because murders and killings are two different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have five minutes. The Defence? The Prosecution? No? The Defence then?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Barucija, when you bumped into the commission in that area and when you participated for a very brief period of time in that conversation with them, what was your conclusion after that? Why did the commission come in the first place?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: Our conclusion was that they were here to inspect the village, because rumour had it that the village had been torched. And as for the word "massacre," I first heard it from the representatives of the HVO. The others didn't mention any such thing. Whatever they asked us, whatever short questions they put to us, we told them and then we scattered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barucija, in your previous answers, you said that you went to the ground three or four days after the end of the combat operations in order to set up the defence lines, that it was then that you came across this commission. The Judge showed you a statement of a witness speaking about the incident which took place on the 11th of February. Since the defence lines had been established by then, can you remember whether this was closer to the 26th or closer to mid-February?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I believe that it was closer to the 11th of February. If this was stated by somebody who had connections with Milica Kegelj, who was a member of the commission, I'm sure that they will remember things better than I do, but I believe it was rather closer to mid-February than closer to mid-November -- mid-January. We took several days to set up the defence lines and inspected the ground on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you whether you went to a -- you saw more than one commissions on the ground, a member of which would also be Milica Kegelj, could you tell us whether you came across such a commission only once or on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were more than one commissions. I saw Ms. Kegelj only once, on that occasion that I've described.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: If there were a report by an international organisation speaking about a visit that took place towards the end of January, would you be able to remember when this would have been? When was it that you came across this commission?

utterances.speaker: HAZIM BARUCIJA
utterances.text: I can't be sure. It was maybe a few days later. Maybe five or six days later. Maybe it was even 15 days later, as it is stated in your other source. I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Sir, I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague to testify. You have answered all the questions put to you. On behalf of the Chamber, I wish you a happy journey back home and success in your professional career. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that the Defence has an issue to raise, but if it is not urgent, maybe we can put it forward for Monday. We have to go into private session first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has applied for permission to reply to a response made by the Prosecution. The Chamber, which heard the arguments of both parties, believes that there's no reason to authorise such a reply, as the Chamber is fully informed of the problem. So the permission is not granted for a reply. It is ten to two. The hearing for today is over. We will resume work on Monday at 2.15. Thank you.
